questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) and Minimum Bactericidal Concentration (MBC) accurately distinguishes bactericidal from bacteriostatic drugs?

options.label: A
options.text: Bactericidal drugs have a narrower range between MIC and MBC than bacteriostatic drugs

options.label: B
options.text: Bacteriostatic drugs show a higher MIC to MBC ratio than bactericidal drugs

options.label: C
options.text: Both drug types have similar MIC but different MBC values

options.label: D
options.text: Bactericidal drugs have higher MIC but lower MBC values than bacteriostatic drugs

questions.answerText: Bactericidal drugs have a narrower range between MIC and MBC than bacteriostatic drugs
questions.solutionHtml:
2c0716927771822d4942335e">bacteriostatic drugs

Explanation:

Bactericidal drugs often have a smaller difference between the MIC (the concentration required to inhibit bacterial growth) and MBC (the concentration required to kill bacteria) than bacteriostatic drugs. This indicates a more potent killing effect at concentrations close to those needed to inhibit growth.

Bacteriostatic agents inhibit bacterial growth, typically measured by the Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC), while bactericidal agents kill bacteria, usually measured by the Minimum Bactericidal Concentration (MBC). In other words, bacteriostatic prevents further growth, while bactericidal directly eliminates bacteria.

Bacteriostatic

Bactericidal
  • MIC<<<MBC
  • Bacterial growth is restricted but not killed
  • The remaining bacteria are killed by the immunity of the body
  • Examples- Tetracyclines, macrolides
  • MIC = MBC
  • Bacteria are completely killed
  • Examples- Beta-lactams, Fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides

questions.answerText: Extended inhibition of bacterial regrowth post-antibiotic clearance
questions.solutionHtml:
dd16927771990b50bda606">suppression of bacterial growth or a delay in bacterial regrowth after a period of exposure to antibiotics, even after the drugs have been eliminated from the body.

Concentration-dependent killing (CDK)
  • Represents the dose of antimicrobials above MIC that can kill the microbe
  • It is a single high-dose
  • Examples- Aminoglycosides and metronidazole

Time-dependent killing (TDK)
  • Represents the duration over a longer period of time for antimicrobials to kill the bacteria
  • It is multiple daily doses.
  • Examples- Penicillin, Azithromycin

CTDK (combination of CDK &TDK)
  • CTDK is also known as area-dependent killing.
  • Examples- Vancomycin, Fluoroquinolones

Post Antibiotic Effect (PAE)
  • Prolonged suppression of bacterial growth after antibiotic exposure, even when drug levels fall below MIC, due to the body's immune response.
  • Advantage: Duration of therapy can be reduced.
  • E.g. In TB, Rifampicin is given once a day due to its CDK property, but in leprosy, it is given once a month to utilise its PAE effectively.

questions.stem: Which statement is true about acquired resistance?

options.label: A
options.text: It depends on both the microorganism and the drug

options.label: B
options.text: It depends only on the microorganism

options.label: C
options.text: It depends only on the drug

options.label: D
options.text: It is independent of the microorganism and the drug

questions.answerText: It depends on both the microorganism and the drug
questions.solutionHtml:
>microorganism to an antimicrobial agent (AMA). It depends on both the microorganism and the drug. There are 2 types:

Natural resistance

Acquired resistance

Some microbes lack the metabolic process or target site the particular drug affects

Development of resistance by an organism (sensitive before) due to the use of an AMA over a period of time

e.g.

  • gram-negative bacilli are unaffected by penicillin G
  • aerobic organisms are not affected by metronidazole
  • anaerobic bacteria are not inhibited by aminoglycoside antibiotics

The development of resistance is dependent on the microorganism as well as on the drug.

Some bacteria rapidly acquire resistance,

e.g. staphylococci, coliforms, tubercle bacilli, gonococci

This does not pose a significant clinical problem

This can happen with any microbe and is a major clinical problem
 

They are of 2 types

  • Mutation
  • Gene transfer

 



Essentials of Medical Pharmacology- K.D Tripathi, 8th Edition, Page 742

questions.stem: The transfer of antimicrobial resistance through a virus called bacteriophage is called?
questions.solutionHtml:
tomMeta" data-dictid="78d28b340916927771810a3fffeb0a">antimicrobial resistance through the agency of a bacteriophage. It is a type of gene transfer.

Mutation

Gene transfer

It is a stable and heritable genetic change that occurs spontaneously and randomly among microorganisms

The gene that causes resistance is passed from one organism to another

Vertical transfer of resistance; relatively slow and usually of lower grade

Horizontal transfer of resistance; rapid spread; high-level resistance to several antibiotics

There are 2 types

  • Single step: A single gene mutation confers high resistance, emerging rapidly (e.g., enterococci to streptomycin)
  • Multistep: Several gene modifications are involved; sensitivity decreases gradually stepwise. (e.g., resistance to erythromycin, tetracyclines and chloramphenicol) (Option D)

There are 3 types

  • Conjugation: One bacteria acquires a resistance gene from another bacteria via plasmid (e.g., MDR TB, typhoid)(Option A)
  • Transduction: Bacteria acquire resistance genes from a bacteriophage (e.g., MRSA)
  • Transformation-Bacteria acquire genes directly from the environment (e.g., pneumococci, gonococci)(Option C)

TRANSDUCTION

 





Essentials of Medical Pharmacology- K.D Tripathi, 8th Edition, Page 742-743

questions.stem: Bacteria lacking a cell wall, such as Mycoplasma species, primarily exhibit resistance through which mechanism?
questions.solutionHtml:
the uptake of antimicrobial agents (AMAs) into the cell (Drug influx)

There are 4 main causes of antimicrobial resistance.

 

Description

Examples

Drug Efflux

(Option A)

Bacteria possess efflux pumps to expel toxic substances and antimicrobial agents (AMAs)

Antimalarials (chloroquine), Tetracyclines, Tigecycline

Drug Influx

(Option B)

Natural mechanisms in bacteria prevent the uptake of AMAs

Mycoplasma (resistant to β-lactams and glycopeptides due to lack of cell wall)

Enzyme inactivation

(Option C)

Bacterial enzymes like β-lactamases inactivate β-lactam drugs by hydrolysing a specific site in their ring structure

β-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins), Aminoglycosides, Chloramphenicol

Mutation in target

(Option D)

Bacteria modify components of their cell to resist AMAs

β-lactam resistance in gram-positive bacteria via altered penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), Fluoroquinolones (DNA gyrase mutation), Vancomycin (van genes altering peptidoglycan precursors)

questions.stem: When combining a bactericidal and bacteriostatic drug, what is the most likely outcome?

options.label: C
options.text: Both Drug antagonism and drug synergism

options.label: D
options.text: Neither Drug antagonism nor drug synergism

questions.solutionHtml:
:collapse; width:777px">

Drug synergism (Option B)

Drug antagonism (Option A)

Supra-additive effect when different antimicrobial agents (AMAs) are combined, enhancing efficacy beyond individual effects.
 

  • Sequential enzyme block:
    E.g.,Sulfonamide + trimethoprim: Sequentially blocks bacterial folate metabolism, leading to cidal action together compared to static effects individually.
     
  • Block drug inactivating enzyme:
    E.g., Ampicillin + Sulbactam: β-lactamases block ampicillin but sulbactam blocks β-lactamases.
     
  • Increase entry of the drug into microbes:
    E.g., Cell wall synthesis inhibitors increase the entry of aminoglycosides (Ceftazidime enhances gentamicin penetration against Pseudomonas).

When two AMAs belonging to different classes are used together, they sometimes have a negative effect on each other.

 
  • Bactericidal + Bacteriostatic: Combining them may diminish the effect of bacteriostatic drugs. E.g., penicillin + tetracycline/chloramphenicol against pneumococci can increase mortality rates compared to penicillin alone.
     
  • Penicillin can deactivate aminoglycosides when both are present together.
     
  • Bacteria can produce beta-lactamases that degrade other beta-lactam antibiotics when used in combination.


Essentials of Medical Pharmacology- K.D Tripathi, 8th Edition, Page 749-750
